title: Database & Transaction Thinking

topics.title: Relational modeling
topics.description: Relational modeling organizes facts into rows with explicit relationships and constraints.
learningGoals: Relationships and cardinalities are explicit
Repeated facts have a consistency plan
examples: A user owns several sessions.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Relational modeling organizes facts into rows with explicit relationships and constraints. Avoid repeating one fact in many places unless you also define how consistency is maintained. Model access patterns after defining domain meaning.

workedExample.scenario: A user owns several sessions.
steps: Store user facts once in users.
Sessions reference the user's ID.

commonMistakes: A table for every class is not automatically a good relational model.
material.independentExercise: Model reservations and stock while naming every relationship.
recallQuestions: Which facts have one owner?
Which duplication creates update anomalies?

acceptanceCriteria: Relationships and cardinalities are explicit
Repeated facts have a consistency plan

topics.title: Primary keys
topics.description: A primary key uniquely identifies a row and is non-null.
learningGoals: Row identity survives attribute changes
Business uniqueness is enforced separately
examples: A user changes email.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies a row and is non-null. Prefer an identity that remains stable as other attributes change. Choosing a generated ID does not remove the need for separate business uniqueness constraints.

workedExample.scenario: A user changes email.
steps: Its user ID remains stable.
Session references still identify the same user.

commonMistakes: A generated primary key does not prevent duplicate business records.
guidedExercise: Choose keys for three auth tables
material.independentExercise: Compare generated IDs with natural keys for coupon codes.
recallQuestions: Which identifier can change?
What does the primary key not guarantee?

acceptanceCriteria: Row identity survives attribute changes
Business uniqueness is enforced separately

topics.title: Foreign keys
topics.description: A foreign key ensures a referenced row exists under the defined constraint.
learningGoals: Orphan rows cannot be inserted
Deletion behavior is tested
examples: A session references a missing user.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A foreign key ensures a referenced row exists under the defined constraint. Decide what happens when the parent is deleted: reject, cascade, or clear the relationship where valid. An application check alone cannot provide the same concurrent guarantee.

workedExample.scenario: A session references a missing user.
steps: The insert is rejected.
Deleting a valid user follows an explicit session policy.

commonMistakes: A foreign key does not automatically choose the right deletion policy.
guidedExercise: Create and violate a session foreign key
material.independentExercise: Design token-to-session relationships without orphan tokens.
recallQuestions: Who enforces parent existence?
What should deletion do to children?

acceptanceCriteria: Orphan rows cannot be inserted
Deletion behavior is tested

topics.title: Unique constraints
topics.description: A unique constraint lets the database arbitrate conflicting writes.
learningGoals: Concurrent duplicates cannot both commit
Conflict behavior is explicit
examples: Two transactions insert the same token hash.

tasks.title: Explain Unique constraints in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A unique constraint lets the database arbitrate conflicting writes. Define the exact columns and treatment of nulls instead of assuming application checks are sufficient. Translate conflicts into a deliberate use-case outcome.

workedExample.scenario: Two transactions insert the same token hash.
steps: One can succeed.
The other receives a uniqueness conflict.

commonMistakes: A preceding existence query cannot prevent a concurrent duplicate insert.
material.independentExercise: Enforce one redemption per user and voucher using a composite constraint.
recallQuestions: What defines the unique business key?
How do nullable values affect uniqueness?

acceptanceCriteria: Concurrent duplicates cannot both commit
Conflict behavior is explicit

topics.title: SQL reads, writes, and parameters

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Write and execute SQL directly before delegating it to an ORM.
learningGoals: Values are parameterized
Missing and conditional-update outcomes are distinguished
examples: Revoke one active session by ID.

material.explanation: Write and execute SQL directly before delegating it to an ORM. Bind untrusted values as parameters, inspect affected-row counts, and distinguish no match from query failure. Update statements should express the intended state condition.

workedExample.scenario: Revoke one active session by ID.
steps: Use a parameter for the ID.
Check whether the update affected zero or one row.

commonMistakes: String concatenation is not safe parameter binding.
guidedExercise: Execute select, insert, update, and delete
material.independentExercise: Write a coupon redemption update that requires remaining uses above zero.
recallQuestions: What does a zero affected-row count mean?
Which query parts cannot be bound as ordinary values?

acceptanceCriteria: Values are parameterized
Missing and conditional-update outcomes are distinguished

topics.title: Joins and aggregation

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Joins combine related rows; aggregation summarizes them.
learningGoals: Zero-child parents are handled deliberately
Multiple children do not corrupt counts
examples: User U1 has two active sessions and U2 has none.

material.explanation: Joins combine related rows; aggregation summarizes them. One-to-many joins can multiply rows, so count the intended entity and understand whether absent children should remain visible. Grouping must match the question being answered.

workedExample.scenario: User U1 has two active sessions and U2 has none.
steps: A left join retains both users.
The chosen count reports 2 and 0.

commonMistakes: Counting joined rows can inflate totals or count a null placeholder.
material.independentExercise: List users with no active sessions and verify the result using fixtures.
recallQuestions: Which rows disappear in an inner join?
What exactly does your count measure?

acceptanceCriteria: Zero-child parents are handled deliberately
Multiple children do not corrupt counts

topics.title: Indexes
topics.description: Indexes can accelerate matching, ordering, and joining but consume storage and write effort.
learningGoals: Each index has a concrete query justification
Read and write tradeoffs are documented
examples: Query sessions by user and recent activity.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Indexes can accelerate matching, ordering, and joining but consume storage and write effort. Choose them from actual queries and inspect plans. A foreign key does not automatically imply the referencing-side index you need.

workedExample.scenario: Query sessions by user and recent activity.
steps: Consider a matching composite index.
Compare the plan on realistic data.

commonMistakes: An index on every column can make writes expensive without improving key queries.
guidedExercise: Propose indexes from predicates and order
material.independentExercise: Measure a token-hash lookup and a session-list query.
recallQuestions: Which query benefits from this index?
What cost does every write pay?

acceptanceCriteria: Each index has a concrete query justification
Read and write tradeoffs are documented

topics.title: Pagination and query plans

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Pagination needs a deterministic order, usually with a unique tie-breaker.
learningGoals: No ties create duplicate or missing rows in a static dataset
The plan is interpreted using real row counts
examples: List sessions ordered by created_at and id.

material.explanation: Pagination needs a deterministic order, usually with a unique tie-breaker. Offset pages can drift under concurrent writes; keyset cursors follow the last observed key. Query plans show chosen work, not a guarantee that the query is cheap.

workedExample.scenario: List sessions ordered by created_at and id.
steps: Carry both last values in a cursor.
Fetch rows beyond that boundary.

commonMistakes: LIMIT without a stable order is not repeatable pagination.
material.independentExercise: Inspect EXPLAIN for the query; use ANALYZE only when its execution is safe.
recallQuestions: Why is a tie-breaker needed?
What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually do?

acceptanceCriteria: No ties create duplicate or missing rows in a static dataset
The plan is interpreted using real row counts

topics.title: Transactions
topics.description: A transaction groups related database changes into one commit or rollback.
learningGoals: An injected failure leaves neither partial change committed
Success commits the complete unit
examples: Revoke X and insert replacement Y.

tasks.title: Explain Transactions in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A transaction groups related database changes into one commit or rollback. Know the connection's autocommit behavior and ensure every statement participates in the intended transaction. Database atomicity does not include arbitrary external API calls.

workedExample.scenario: Revoke X and insert replacement Y.
steps: If insertion fails, roll back revocation.
On success commit both changes.

commonMistakes: Placing statements near each other does not make them atomic.
material.independentExercise: Reserve stock and record the reservation in one atomic unit.
recallQuestions: Which connection owns the transaction?
What side effects cannot roll back with it?

acceptanceCriteria: An injected failure leaves neither partial change committed
Success commits the complete unit

topics.title: ACID
topics.description: ACID names related transaction properties, not a promise that business logic is automatically correct.
learningGoals: Each property has a concrete scenario
Business rules are not delegated to the acronym
examples: Record a reservation and decrement stock.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: ACID names related transaction properties, not a promise that business logic is automatically correct. Constraints help consistency; isolation controls concurrent observations; durability depends on configured persistence guarantees. Translate each property into a concrete failure scenario.

workedExample.scenario: Record a reservation and decrement stock.
steps: Atomicity prevents only one write committing.
Constraints and isolation still matter for valid stock.

commonMistakes: ACID does not invent your missing business invariant.
guidedExercise: Explain each property using reservation examples
Identify the application rules still needed
material.independentExercise: Classify failure cases as atomicity, consistency, isolation, or durability concerns.
recallQuestions: Which property prevents partial commit?
Why can a transaction still contain wrong logic?

acceptanceCriteria: Each property has a concrete scenario
Business rules are not delegated to the acronym

topics.title: Isolation levels
topics.description: Isolation determines what concurrent transactions may observe.
learningGoals: The observed interleaving is documented
The chosen protection matches the invariant
examples: Two reads run in one Read Committed transaction.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Isolation determines what concurrent transactions may observe. PostgreSQL commonly uses Read Committed, with a fresh snapshot per statement; stronger levels change behavior and may require retries. Test actual interleavings instead of assuming a transaction serializes everything.

workedExample.scenario: Two reads run in one Read Committed transaction.
steps: Another transaction commits between them.
The second statement may see newer committed data.

commonMistakes: A transaction does not automatically provide one immutable snapshot.
guidedExercise: Record observations at two isolation levels
material.independentExercise: Explain which isolation or conditional write protects a stock reservation.
recallQuestions: What does a statement snapshot mean?
When can a stronger level require retry?

acceptanceCriteria: The observed interleaving is documented
The chosen protection matches the invariant

topics.title: Race conditions
topics.description: A race arises when overlapping operations invalidate assumptions between reads and writes.
learningGoals: Exactly one reservation succeeds for one available unit
The loser causes no partial write
examples: A and B see one item available.

tasks.title: Explain Race conditions in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: A race arises when overlapping operations invalidate assumptions between reads and writes. Write the interleaving explicitly, then move the decision into a protected transaction or atomic conditional statement. A delayed sleep is not proof of correctness.

workedExample.scenario: A and B see one item available.
steps: Both try to reserve it.
A conditional decrement permits only the transaction that finds stock above zero.

commonMistakes: Checking stock in Java and updating later leaves a race window.
guidedExercise: Replace it with a conditional update
material.independentExercise: Use two connections and a start barrier to test the last-item race.
recallQuestions: Which assumption becomes stale?
How does the losing caller learn it lost?

acceptanceCriteria: Exactly one reservation succeeds for one available unit
The loser causes no partial write

topics.title: Optimistic locking
topics.description: Optimistic locking detects that state changed since it was read.
learningGoals: Stale updates cannot overwrite newer state
Conflict and retry outcomes are explicit
examples: Both callers read version 3.

tasks.title: Explain Optimistic locking in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Optimistic locking detects that state changed since it was read. Include an expected version in the update and check the affected-row count. Decide whether to retry the whole use case or return a conflict; never silently overwrite the newer state.

workedExample.scenario: Both callers read version 3.
steps: A writes version 4 conditionally.
B's version-3 update affects zero rows.

commonMistakes: A version column does nothing unless updates check it.
material.independentExercise: Protect concurrent account updates and define a bounded retry policy.
recallQuestions: What does a version conflict mean?
When is retrying unsafe?

acceptanceCriteria: Stale updates cannot overwrite newer state
Conflict and retry outcomes are explicit

topics.title: Pessimistic locking
topics.description: Pessimistic locking reserves access to conflicting rows during a transaction.
learningGoals: Validation uses the protected current state
External waiting is excluded from lock scope
examples: A locks token X for rotation.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Pessimistic locking reserves access to conflicting rows during a transaction. Acquire locks in a consistent order and keep the transaction short. Waiting on an external API while holding a row lock can amplify contention and failure.

workedExample.scenario: A locks token X for rotation.
steps: B waits for the lock.
After A commits, B must re-evaluate X's changed state.

commonMistakes: Getting the lock does not mean earlier validation is still valid.
guidedExercise: Measure what happens to the second connection
material.independentExercise: Reserve stock with row locking and compare it to a conditional update.
recallQuestions: When are row locks released?
What must be rechecked after waiting?

acceptanceCriteria: Validation uses the protected current state
External waiting is excluded from lock scope

topics.title: Deadlocks
topics.description: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle.
learningGoals: Lock order is consistent
A deadlock failure does not produce partial committed work
examples: A locks account 1 then requests 2.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle. Use consistent acquisition order to reduce risk and recognize that a database may abort a participant. Recovery must restart a valid unit of work, not continue an aborted transaction.

workedExample.scenario: A locks account 1 then requests 2.
steps: B locks 2 then requests 1.
Ordering both by ID avoids that particular cycle.

commonMistakes: Short transactions can still deadlock if lock order conflicts.
material.independentExercise: Test two opposing transfers with bounded recovery after an aborted transaction.
recallQuestions: What creates the cycle?
What must be retried after an abort?

acceptanceCriteria: Lock order is consistent
A deadlock failure does not produce partial committed work

topics.title: JDBC and repository adapters

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: JDBC makes SQL execution, transactions, and resource ownership visible.
learningGoals: Resources close on both paths
SQL and database types remain inside the adapter
examples: Find a token by hash.

material.explanation: JDBC makes SQL execution, transactions, and resource ownership visible. A repository adapter translates rows and database failures into its contract. Close connections, statements, and result sets appropriately; do not leak database types into domain policy.

workedExample.scenario: Find a token by hash.
steps: Bind the hash in a prepared statement.
Map one row and close resources, or report absence.

commonMistakes: Returning an open ResultSet shifts hidden resource obligations to callers.
guidedExercise: Test empty, duplicate, and unavailable-store behavior
material.independentExercise: Run repository contract tests against an in-memory store and PostgreSQL.
recallQuestions: Who owns the connection?
Which failures belong in the repository contract?

acceptanceCriteria: Resources close on both paths
SQL and database types remain inside the adapter

topics.title: Migrations and integration tests

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: Migrations make schema changes ordered and reviewable.
learningGoals: An empty database reaches the expected schema
Real constraints and transaction rollback are tested
examples: Create users, sessions, and tokens from migrations.

material.explanation: Migrations make schema changes ordered and reviewable. Test them on an empty database and validate the resulting constraints with a real engine. In-memory fakes cannot prove actual SQL syntax, locking, or constraint behavior.

workedExample.scenario: Create users, sessions, and tokens from migrations.
steps: Run against a fresh database.
Attempt invalid and duplicate rows.

commonMistakes: A passing fake-repository test does not validate PostgreSQL behavior.
guidedExercise: Apply schema migrations from empty state
material.independentExercise: Use Testcontainers for a reproducible repository integration check.
recallQuestions: What does an integration test prove beyond a unit test?
How can a migration break an existing database?

acceptanceCriteria: An empty database reaches the expected schema
Real constraints and transaction rollback are tested

challenges.title: Last Item Reservation

tasks.title: Verify: Exactly one of two competitors succeeds
Verify: Final availability is zero with exactly one active reservation
Verify: Injected failure rolls back both changes
Verify: Duplicate request behavior does not decrement stock twice

challenges.description: Prove a stock invariant with two competing real database transactions.
learningGoals: Prove a stock invariant with two competing real database transactions.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: Stock starts at one.
requirements: One available item and two simultaneous reservation requests
Exactly one request can create an active reservation
The losing request leaves no partial reservation or stock change
Choose a conditional update or row-lock strategy and justify it
Give each request a duplicate identity and define retry behavior
Record affected rows, commits, and rejected outcomes
constraints: A JVM lock alone is not a solution
Use a barrier or controlled interleaving, not timing luck

material.explanation: Use a non-authentication domain to prove transaction reasoning transfers. The admission decision and reservation creation must agree. Write the unsafe schedule first, then show why the chosen database mechanism yields a single winner.

workedExample.scenario: Stock starts at one.
steps: A and B start competing transactions.
One commits a reservation and zero availability; the other cannot reserve a second item.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Create minimal stock and reservation tables.
Force two connections to compete and inspect final rows.
material.independentExercise: Inject failure after decreasing stock but before creating the reservation and verify rollback.
recallQuestions: What selects the winner?
Which two writes must commit together?

acceptanceCriteria: Exactly one of two competitors succeeds
Final availability is zero with exactly one active reservation
Injected failure rolls back both changes
Duplicate request behavior does not decrement stock twice

challenges.title: Concurrent Refresh Rotation
challenges.description: Implement the atomic persistence decision for concurrent refresh and replay handling.
learningGoals: Implement the atomic persistence decision for concurrent refresh and replay handling.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: A consumes X and creates Y.

tasks.title: Transaction boundaries
Locking or atomic update strategy
Unique constraints
Failure and retry behavior
Concurrency test plan
Verify: A parent never has two committed children
Verify: Child-insertion failure preserves the original active parent
Verify: Reuse handling durably applies the declared family policy
Verify: Two-connection tests use controlled coordination
Verify: Lost-response recovery and strict-policy tradeoffs are documented

requirements: Requests A and B both present active token X at nearly the same time
Only one may consume X and persist child Y
Consume parent and create replacement in the same transaction
Revalidate after acquiring any lock or losing a conditional update
Persist lineage so a later replay can identify the active family
If reuse revokes a family, the revocation must commit even though the public operation rejects
Specify response-loss behavior under the chosen strict or bounded-retry policy
constraints: Use real PostgreSQL and separate connections
No single-instance lock as the primary guarantee
Do not return or persist raw tokens in diagnostic evidence
deliverables: Schema and atomic SQL or locking strategy

material.explanation: This challenge turns the earlier algorithm into a real persistence guarantee. Pay particular attention to security mutations during rejected requests: throwing an exception inside a rollback boundary can accidentally undo family revocation. Verify durable final state, not just one successful response.

workedExample.scenario: A consumes X and creates Y.
steps: B then observes X as consumed.
Under strict reuse handling, B commits revocation of the affected family and returns a safe rejection.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Create the lineage schema and constraints.
Test both the winning rotation and durable reuse response.
material.independentExercise: Fail child insertion and prove parent consumption rolls back; separately prove a replay rejection does not roll back required family revocation.
recallQuestions: What happens after a caller waits for the lock?
Can a rejected response still require a committed security change?

acceptanceCriteria: A parent never has two committed children
Child-insertion failure preserves the original active parent
Reuse handling durably applies the declared family policy
Two-connection tests use controlled coordination
Lost-response recovery and strict-policy tradeoffs are documented
